title: Friday: the hour of answer
hookLine: an hour on Friday when du'a is answered (Bukhari)
tomorrow: what does a Friday sound like, counted on ten fingers?

cards: A sale drops at a random minute, and people refresh all day so they don't miss it. Friday has an older version.

In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ speaks of an hour on Friday: if a Muslim standing in prayer asks God for something good in it, God gives it. Then he gestures with his hand, showing how short it is.
And the report never says when.

teach.h: ABU MUSA: PULPIT TO PRAYER'S END.
teach.b: Two answers, each with a report behind it. The first comes from Abu Musa, in Sahih Muslim: the hour falls between the moment the imam sits on the pulpit and the end of the prayer. Its case is simple and strong.
That's when the community is gathered, listening, already in worship. If any stretch of Friday is open, why not the one where everyone stands together?
The second comes from Jabir, in Sunan Abi Dawud: seek it in the last hour of Friday, after 'Asr, before sunset. There's an objection.
The report says standing in prayer, and after 'Asr is a time when voluntary prayer isn't made.
A companion, Abdullah ibn Salam, gave the reply people still quote: whoever sits waiting for the prayer is counted as in prayer.
So someone sitting with their du'a in the late afternoon, waiting for Maghrib, is inside the promise. Scholars gathered these two views, and others besides.
Some concluded the hour is hidden on purpose, the way someone who doesn't know which minute matters stays awake for all of them.
And some people simply keep both windows: quiet attention during the sermon, and du'a in the last light before sunset.
That's the hidden hour: not a code to crack, but a reason to keep asking.

how: Muslims who seek the Friday hour make du'a during the sermon and prayer, and again in the late afternoon after 'Asr, some sitting quietly in the mosque or at home until Maghrib.

o: the hour of the weekly sermon, when talking is banned
Friday, with a short hour when good du'a is answered
a monthly night of prayer kept at the mosque

games.q: two answers for one hour — tap the pairs.
p: imam sits, to the prayer's end
showed how short the hour is

s: the main report gives the Friday hour an exact time
in Bukhari's report he shows how short it is with his hand, but never says when.
one view places the hour in the last stretch before sunset
Jabir's report, in Sunan Abi Dawud: seek it after 'Asr.
if you missed the sermon, the hour is gone for that week
the after-'Asr view keeps the late afternoon open.

games.q: your friend is sure the hour is during the sermon and says the after-'Asr view makes no sense. what's that view's best case?
o: Jabir's report names the last hour, and waiting for prayer counts as prayer.
more people are free later in the day, so it's easier to ask then.
the sermon is too busy for du'a, so the hour must be some other time.
games.why: the after-'Asr view rests on Jabir's report and on Abdullah ibn Salam's answer: whoever sits waiting for the prayer is in prayer.

practice: Take a pen and write, by hand, one good thing you'd ask for if you knew the hour had come. Keep it short and honest.
If you pray, keep the paper for Friday's last light; if not, keep it where you'll see it, as a note of what you're hoping for.

wordCard.voice: Friday's hidden hour: a short time, unnamed in the main report, when a sincere du'a is answered; the reports point to two windows.

orig.note: Arabic: sa'ah, an hour, or a short stretch of time; the word in the Friday report.

carryVoice: One to keep: the hidden hour isn't a code to crack, it's a reason to keep asking. Day three of the week, done.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 935 (an hour on Friday; a Muslim standing in prayer asking for good is given it; he pointed with his hand to show how short it is)
Sahih Muslim 853 (Abu Musa: between the imam sitting and the end of the prayer)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1048 (Jabir: seek it in the last hour after 'Asr)
Sunan Abi Dawud 1046; Muwatta Malik, Book of Friday (Abdullah ibn Salam: whoever sits waiting for the prayer is in prayer)
Sahih al-Bukhari 586 (no voluntary prayer after 'Asr until sunset)
